title: Climate Watchdog Grilled on Net Zero Progress
label: 9 September 2026 · Climate Change Committee evidence
summary: The Environmental Audit Committee questioned Emma Pinchbeck and Dr Eoin Devane of the Climate Change Committee on the UK's progress in cutting emissions. The session covered delays in advising on Heathrow expansion, the demand for faster electrification, the role of electric vehicles and heat pumps, grid capacity, industrial decarbonisation, and land use and agriculture. The main conclusion was that while some sectors are doing well, the Government's plans risk missing the 2030 international commitment and rely too heavily on risky technologies like carbon capture and removals.

chapters.title: Heathrow Advice Delay
chapters.takeaway: The CCC is late publishing its advice on Heathrow expansion, blaming limited resources and wanting to avoid party conference season.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Emma, your committee was asked last November for views on the airports national policy statement and Heathrow. Why did it take over six months to reply, and why won't the advice be published until after the consultation closes?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We're a small body and we had a new chair and statutory adaptation advice to publish. We're independent, so it's not our job to shape the consultation, but we did have working-level talks with officials. We'll publish in a couple of weeks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But the public and Parliament won't see your views before the consultation closes. That undermines your role as the independent adviser to Parliament. How will you help us scrutinise the final policy before Parliament votes?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We'll provide the draft advice on publication and then be available to parliamentarians in formal sessions or informally. We're not planning extra modelling beyond that.

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Our advice next week will assess the draft and recommend changes. We don't have a statutory role on national policy statements; we were commissioned specifically for this.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I worry resource constraints are hampering your statutory role. Perhaps the Chair should write to the Department or Treasury about this.

chapters.title: Good News and Key Messages
chapters.takeaway: The CCC highlights positive trends like EV uptake and renewables, but urges the new government to speed up electrification and make electricity cheaper.

turns.speaker: Dr Roz Savage
turns.text: With a new Prime Minister and new Secretaries of State, what are your key messages for staying on track with climate targets?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Good news first: EVs are booming—a quarter of new car sales are electric. Renewables hit records, and peatland restoration is up 24%. Emissions have halved since 2008. Households with an EV, heat pump, solar and a smart tariff save around £1,200 a year compared to fossil fuels. But we need more electrification. The government's plan risks missing the 2030 international commitment if they don't speed up.

turns.speaker: Dr Roz Savage
turns.text: What about nature and DEFRA?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Tree planting rates have fallen by 25%, largely due to a Scottish policy change. We need a big increase. But the land use framework and sustainable farming roadmap are positive steps.

chapters.title: Cutting Electricity Prices
chapters.takeaway: The gap between electricity and gas prices remains too wide, and the VAT cut alone isn't enough to drive electrification.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: The PM cut VAT on electricity. What impact will that have?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: It'll help a bit—Ofgem says bills would have been £45 higher without it. But the ratio of electricity to gas prices is still around 3.3 to 1. We need it below 3 to make efficient technologies pay off. Removing remaining levies would bring it to about 3 to 1. It's a start, but not enough.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: What about new North Sea drilling?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: North Sea emissions aren't fully in our carbon budgets. Reserves are in steep decline anyway—production is expected to fall 93% by 2050. The basin needs a transition plan for jobs. The fastest way to cut bills is to electrify and reduce gas demand, not increase supply. Faster electrification could save £8 billion.

chapters.title: Technology vs Behaviour Change
chapters.takeaway: The government's pathway relies more on technology and removals, which carries risks and needs better monitoring and contingency plans.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: The government's plan relies more on technology and less on behaviour change. What risks does that create?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: About a third of their pathway involves household choices, but they go slower on EVs and heat pumps and predict higher aviation demand. They rely on removals for 17% of emissions cuts between 2031 and 2037. That's not unreasonable, but they need clear pathways, monitoring, and contingency plans if tech doesn't deliver.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: Do they adequately consider that delaying investment increases long-term costs?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: No. If you can access these technologies today, you save money. Delaying prevents households from saving. Even with slower rollout, we found every £1 spent on net zero returns £2 to £4 in benefits. Going faster is better.

chapters.title: Datacentres and Grid Pressure
chapters.takeaway: Massive datacentre demand could strain the grid, and on-site fossil fuel generation poses a risk to carbon budgets.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: Datacentres are demanding huge amounts of electricity—some 80 GW of connections. Are you worried about crowding out renewable power for others?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We included National Grid's top estimate for datacentre demand in our modelling, plus headroom. So we've advised on an energy system of the right dimensions. But there are policy questions about where to locate them and how to bring them on. It's early days; we're keeping it under review.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: Many datacentres are building on-site fossil fuel generation. Two planned sites could exceed ExxonMobil's UK emissions. Isn't that a huge risk to carbon budgets?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: If significant fossil fuel build-out shows up in our inventory, we'll look at it for the eighth carbon budget. But decisions about planning and industrial strategy are for government. We'll hold them to account on emissions.

chapters.title: Electric Vehicles and Costs
chapters.takeaway: The ZEV mandate is working but could be improved; weakening it would undermine the 2030 commitment and consumer savings.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: If the ZEV mandate were weakened, would that undermine progress?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Yes, seriously. EV transition is the biggest emissions reduction measure in the government's plan—about a fifth of cuts to 2030. Weakening it would make the 2030 NDC nearly impossible and send a troubling message. The mandate could be improved to stop over-rewarding plug-in hybrids, but it's working. Manufacturers met targets in 2024 and 2025.

turns.speaker: Sammy Wilson
turns.text: But the mandate is costing manufacturers billions in discounts and hurting the industry. How long can we sustain this?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Manufacturers discount all cars, not just EVs. Competition is good for consumers. The EU also has EV targets, and over three-quarters of UK-made cars are exported. We need to produce EVs to compete.

turns.speaker: Sammy Wilson
turns.text: With vehicle excise duty on EVs, will they still be attractive?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Yes. EVs are so much more efficient that even with a like-for-like fuel duty, you'd save on running costs. The proposed eVED is less than half the per-mile fuel duty, so savings remain.

chapters.title: Heat Pumps and Homes
chapters.takeaway: Heat pump rollout is lagging, and the Warm Homes Plan needs longer-term funding and consumer protections to succeed.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: How can we ensure the Warm Homes Plan avoids botched installations and delivers for low-income homes?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: We need about 37% annual growth in heat pump installations, but last year growth was only 7%, down from 56%. The fall was driven by low-income installations through ECO. We're concerned about the lack of clarity on future funding. We need proper certification, consumer protections, and a simpler journey.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: Air-to-air heat pumps are cheaper. Should the government promote them more?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Yes, they can also provide cooling. But there are no certified installers under the MCS for the grant yet—that needs to change soon. Once it does, people can get £2,500 grants, plus low-income support.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: What about making people aware of the lower costs?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Public information campaigns are good. A third of householders are open to heat pumps, but only 2% have one. Friends and family are the best advisers, so more installations will build confidence.

chapters.title: Industry, Aviation, and Land Use
chapters.takeaway: Industrial electricity prices remain high, SAF scale-up is slow, and land use policies need long-term funding to cut emissions.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: UK industrial electricity prices are high. Is more action needed?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Yes. Supercharger discounts bring the ratio down to 2:1 for 500 companies, but others only get 3.1:1. We need more action and support for up-front capital costs. Scrapping the industrial transformation scheme was a mistake. We need a long-term industrial strategy.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: SAF is only 2.5% of aviation fuel. What should the government do to scale up?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: We need to stick to the mandate targets and set out a clear diversification strategy in the jet zero update. The SAF revenue certainty mechanism is positive; bringing it forward would help.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: Land use emissions have barely fallen. How can the frameworks help?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: The land use framework and farming roadmap are good steps, with funding to 2030. But we need sustained incentives for tree planting and peatland restoration. Tree planting needs to more than double by 2030. Funding certainty beyond 2030 is missing.
